summary: This benchmark investigates whether transplanting a coding expert block into a larger language model enables syntax-rule generalization across counterfactual opening delimiters. Using 256 triplets where only the opening delimiter varies, the study demonstrates that the spliced model fails the syntax transfer task completely (0/256 triplets) due to a heavy parenthesis bias, while donor ablation isolates specific donor-dependent outputs. The negative result is thoroughly documented, rigorously controlled, and methodologically sound.
strengths: Rigorous counterfactual benchmark design isolating delimiter syntax while keeping program suffixes and runtime semantics strictly constant.
Comprehensive control suite including untouched native host, adapted native host, adapted general graft, coding graft, shuffled donor, and donor-off ablation.
Transparent and honest reporting of a clear negative result without attempting to overstate transfer capabilities.
High reproducibility standards with commit-pinned repository links, SHA-256 artifact verification, and complete runtime environment specifications (MLX, Python, hardware).
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is limited to a single host-donor model pair (Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B into Qwen2.5-1.5B) and a single layer insertion point (block 27).
Synthetic arithmetic test cases may not reflect the full complexity and context-handling characteristics of real-world multi-token coding tasks.
The donor-off rescue effect (rescuing 69 braces upon disabling the donor) lacks a deeper mechanistic explanation beyond aggregate repair counts.
suggestions: Extend the counterfactual delimiter benchmark across multiple insertion depths and different donor/host architectural families to test if delimiter blindness is universal in expert splicing.
Provide attention attribution or logit lens analysis to explain why disabling the donor rescues brace repairs that the grafted donor suppresses.
Integrate the code repository directly with the Pubroot platform submission rather than relying on external commit links to qualify for open-code verification badges.

claims.text: The smaller model is Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B. The host is Qwen2.5-1.5B.
Fill-in-the-middle training allows autoregressive language models to learn to infill text by moving a text span from the middle to the end.
A constant suffix-only prediction can solve at most one member per triplet.
claims.source: Logical derivation: each triplet features three distinct opening delimiters requiring three distinct matching closing delimiters with identical suffixes.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Applies fill-in-the-middle program completion within an expert-splicing interpretability benchmark rather than as a general pretraining objective.
